title: Collage
description: Collage cinematography builds a frame from torn, cut, or mixed pieces: different stocks, paper, print, and live action sharing one plane with visible joins. Edges are graphic, and the stack is a construction, not an optical blend.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: A head from one still, a building from another, newsprint, a painted sky. You can see the scissors.
Mixed grain, mixed contrast, maybe a bit of tape. One image was not enough, so the frame was assembled.

Use it when sources should remain sources: titles, satire, memory as scrapbook, a graphic sequence that refuses photographic unity. It is the wrong tool when two photographs should fuse as density (double exposure) or when live action and animation share a photographed space without torn edges.
Mixed media can do either. Collage insists on the cut.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: Shoot or collect plates. Cut them.
Leave borders, torn fiber, misregistered printing, different grain structures. Composite with hard or torn masks, not a screen blend.
Prompt: torn layers, mixed stocks, cut paper and live action sharing one plane, visible joins, not a smooth double exposure.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: A portrait built from a live face, a city fragment, and newsprint, joins visible. Do not dissolve the same elements into a ghosted overlay and call it collage.

sections.title: Compared with similar shots

blocks.text: Double Exposure is an optical or additive stack without scissors. Mixed Media is the broader family (animation plus live, print plus plate).
Collage is the cut-and-paste grammar inside that family. Split Screen divides the frame into simultaneous pictures with a designed border, usually live.
Collage can ignore a shared timebase.
Mixed MediaNo single medium owns the truth.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: Terry Gilliam's Monty Python work is cut-out collage in motion. The Jinx titles treat documents and images as a stacked graphic plane.
Bruce Conner's A Movie is found-footage collage as a film, which is grammar for the cut, not a look to clone.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: Wrong cousin: double exposure or a clean split-screen. Tell: translucent blend, matching grain across pieces, or a hard live divider without paper or tear.
Fix: mismatched stocks, torn or cut borders, graphic stacking.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is collage in film?
A frame assembled from cut or torn pieces of different images and materials, with joins meant to be seen. It is construction, not a seamless composite.
Collage vs double exposure
Double exposure blends records as density. Collage keeps edges: scissors, paper, mixed stocks. One is optical stack. The other is cut and paste.
When should I use collage?
When one photograph is not enough and the sources should stay visible. Do not use it for a ghosted memory overlay or a seamless twin shot.
How do I prompt collage for AI image or video?
Ask for torn layers, mixed film stocks or paper, live action plus cut pieces, and visible joins. Ban smooth double exposure.
